content_voiceover: This slide illustrates the concept of an ideal monitoring test using a conceptual graph and a real-world example. On the left, the graph plots test results against actual DOAC drug level. The dashed red diagonal line represents an ideal test, one whose result rises linearly and predictably with drug concentration, so that a given test value always corresponds to a known drug level. The blue shaded box marks the on-therapy drug level range, and the green shaded box marks the normal range of the test, in an ideal world, these would align cleanly so clinicians could infer drug level directly from the test result. On the right, real INR data from five warfarin samples measured with four different thromboplastin reagents, Neoplastine CI, Innovin, Neoplastine CI+, and Recombiplastin, illustrates why this ideal is hard to achieve even for a familiar drug like warfarin, the same sample gives different INR values depending on reagent, and the spread widens at higher INR values. This reagent variability is exactly the kind of problem that plagues DOAC monitoring using routine PT or APTT, since these assays were never designed or calibrated for the mechanism of action of direct factor Xa or thrombin inhibitors, reinforcing why dedicated calibrated assays, like anti-Xa levels, are preferred whenever precise DOAC quantification is needed.
keypoints: An ideal monitoring test shows a linear, predictable relationship with drug level
Routine PT/INR results vary by reagent, shown across four thromboplastin reagents
Reagent-to-reagent INR variability increases at higher drug levels
Routine PT/APTT were not designed for DOAC quantification; calibrated assays are preferred
keypoint_voiceover: Key concepts to remember. An ideal monitoring test has a linear, predictable relationship with actual drug level. Routine PT and INR results vary depending on which thromboplastin reagent is used. This variability grows larger at higher drug concentrations. And because routine PT and APTT were never designed for DOAC quantification, dedicated calibrated assays are preferred when precise levels matter.
